issues.legal_issue: A claim for possession based on title is governed by the limitation period for such claims when the defendant’s possession rests on instruments that are nullities for want of jurisdiction, and a separate declaration invalidating those instruments is unnecessary.
material_facts: The property was within the statutory ceiling limit, and the authority exercised a purchase option under a restriction on transfer that had been held invalid insofar as it applied to property within that limit.
The authority’s order lacked jurisdiction, and the sale deed was executed pursuant to that order; the defendant took possession under those documents.
The claimant sought possession based on title and challenged the order and sale deed in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The order and sale deed were nullities and could be disregarded without first obtaining a separate declaration setting them aside. The claim was governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was within time.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a suit for possession of immovable property based on title is subject to the limitation period running from when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse. Article 58 governs suits to obtain a declaration. An order made without jurisdiction may be ignored as a nullity, without seeking to set it aside, and a suit for possession based on title is governed by Article 65: Ajudh Raj v. Moti. In Maharao Sahib Shri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, Section 27(1) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was held invalid insofar as it restricted transfers of urban property within the ceiling limit.

predicates.suit_for_possession_based_on_title: The claimant brought a suit seeking possession of immovable property on the basis of title.
predicates.defendant_possession_under_instruments: The defendant took or held possession of the property under the challenged instruments.
predicates.instruments_void_for_lack_of_jurisdictio: The instruments on which the defendant’s possession rested were made or executed pursuant to an order that lacked jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks possession based on title and the defendant holds possession under instruments that are jurisdictionally void, the limitation rule for title-based possession claims applies.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant is not barred from obtaining possession on equitable grounds merely because the claimant received and retained consideration under a compelled transfer made pursuant to an invalid order.
material_facts: The claimant did not voluntarily sell the property to the state but executed the sale deed following an order made without jurisdiction.
The claimant received and retained the consideration paid under the sale deed and was willing to return it.
The state retained possession of the property, and the claimant sought possession against repayment of the consideration.
issues.conclusion: Equitable considerations did not justify denying the claimant possession, conditional on repayment of the consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Equitable considerations may be relevant to claims for restitution or refund, but Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India concerned claimants who had passed on the burden of duties and suffered no prejudice or loss. Those principles did not warrant denying relief where the transfer was compelled by an unlawful and jurisdictionally invalid order, the claimant suffered loss, and the state retained possession.

rule.if: appeal_against_possession_decree and transfer_compelled_by_void_order and claimant_retained_consideration and defendant_retained_property

predicates.appeal_against_possession_decree: The case is an appeal challenging a decree granting possession of property to a claimant.
predicates.transfer_compelled_by_void_order: The claimant transferred the property because an authority required the transfer through an order that lacked jurisdiction, rather than through a voluntary sale.
predicates.claimant_retained_consideration: The claimant received and retained the consideration paid for the transfer.
predicates.defendant_retained_property: The defendant continued to retain possession of the property.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a possession decree, when a transfer was compelled by a jurisdictionally void order, the claimant kept the consideration, and the defendant kept the property, equitable considerations do not by themselves defeat possession relief.
